title: Fizz on Threes, Buzz on Fives
statement:
Count from 1 to n out loud, with a twist. Return a list of n strings where entry i − 1 describes the number i:

  • "FizzBuzz" if i is divisible by both 3 and 5,
  • "Fizz" if it is divisible by 3 only,
  • "Buzz" if it is divisible by 5 only,
  • otherwise the number itself as a string, like "7".

examples.why: 3 is a multiple of 3, 5 is a multiple of 5, the rest are written out.
15 is a multiple of both. Checking "divisible by 3" first would print "Fizz" there instead.
Numbers are returned as strings, not as integers.

hints: Loop from 1 to n and decide what to write for each number.
Which rule must you test first? Think about 15.
Either test divisibility by 15 first, or build the word in pieces: add "Fizz" for 3, add "Buzz" for 5, and fall back to the number if nothing was added.

explain.intuition:
This is a warm-up about the order of conditions. The rules overlap: a multiple of 15 is also a multiple of 3 and of 5. An if / else if chain stops at the first match, so the most specific rule has to come first.

A tidier version avoids the overlap. Start with an empty string, append "Fizz" if divisible by 3, append "Buzz" if divisible by 5, and use the number if the string is still empty. Adding a new rule (say "Jazz" for 7) then means adding one line, not rewriting every combination.
pitfalls: Testing 3 or 5 before 15 in an else-if chain, so 15 prints "Fizz".
Pushing the number itself instead of its string form. The list must contain only strings.
Looping from 0, or stopping at n − 1. The count runs from 1 to n inclusive.

solutions.title: Most specific rule first
solutions.idea: Check 15, then 3, then 5, then fall back to the number.

solutions.title: Build the word, with countdowns instead of %
solutions.idea: Keep two counters that hit zero every 3rd and every 5th number. Append each rule's word when its counter fires; an empty word means print the number.

followups: Add a third rule: "Jazz" for multiples of 7. Which version adapts with the smallest change?
Make the rules configurable as a list of (divisor, word) pairs passed in by the caller.
